target_claim: Solution line 0047 claims that for S = {x in R^n : Ax <= b}, the polar is exactly S-polar = {y : y^T a_i <= b_i for all i with b_i > 0} intersect {y : y = lambda a_i, lambda >= 0, for all i with b_i = 0}. This is a directly implementable membership predicate on (A, b, y). Also tested: the intermediate claim on lines 0033-0040 that max{y^T x : a_i^T x <= b_i} = y^T a_i / b_i when b_i > 0.
failing_input: Headline (single row, b_1 > 0, so squarely inside the branch the formula explicitly states): n=1, A=[[-2]], b=[1], i.e. S = {x in R : -2x <= 1} = [-1/2, +inf); candidate y = -2. Second direction, also b_1 > 0: A=[[1]], b=[1], S = (-inf, 1], y = -5 (formula ACCEPTS a non-member; explicit integer witness x = -14 in S with y*x = 70 > 1). Triage p0 construction, b_2 = 0 branch: A=[[1],[-1]], b=[2,0], S = [0,2], y = 2/5. Exhaustive sweeps: 400/558 distinct (A,b) instances mismatch for n=1, m<=3, entries in [-2,2] (84 of them with every b_i > 0); 400/459 for n=2, m<=2, entries in [-1,1] (54 with every b_i > 0).
observed_vs_claimed: A=[[-2]], b=[1], y=-2: solution formula says y NOT in S-polar (it demands y*a_1 = (-2)(-2) = 4 <= b_1 = 1, which fails); exact oracle says y IS in S-polar, since sup_{x >= -1/2} (-2)x = 1 <= 1. A=[[1]], b=[1], y=-5: formula says y IS in S-polar (y*a_1 = -5 <= 1); oracle says NOT, with explicit witness x = -14 in S and y*x = 70 > 1. A=[[1],[-1]], b=[2,0], y=2/5: formula says NOT in S-polar (row 2 has b_2 = 0 and forces y to be a nonnegative multiple of a_2 = -1, i.e. y <= 0); oracle says IS in S-polar, since sup_{x in [0,2]} (2/5)x = 4/5 <= 1. So the claimed set is neither contained in nor contains the true polar. Secondary claim also refuted: for a=(1,0), b=1, y=(0,1) the formula gives max = y^T a / b = 0, but x = (-12, 1) is feasible with y^T x = 1 > 0 (the true sup is +infinity); for a=(1), b=2, y=(1) the formula gives 1/2 but x = 1 is feasible with y^T x = 1 > 1/2. Root cause: the solution treats each row of A in isolation, whereas sup_{x in S} y^T x is a joint LP over all rows; and it asserts the max of y^T x over a single half-space is attained at x = a_i/b_i, which is false whenever y is not a nonnegative multiple of a_i (the sup is then +infinity). The earlier duality/projection argument on lines 0014-0026 is a different, essentially sound route; the refuted material is the 'Alternatively' explicit construction on lines 0027-0049, which the solution presents as an independent proof and as an explicit half-space representation of S-polar.
faithfulness_notes: member_solution() is a literal transcription of line 0047: for each row with b_i > 0 require y^T a_i <= b_i; for each row with b_i = 0 require y = lambda a_i for some lambda >= 0; rows with b_i < 0 are never mentioned by line 0047, so the implementation imposes nothing for them. To keep the refutation independent of that reading, the headline counterexamples were chosen from instances where every b_i > 0, i.e. only the branch the solution explicitly writes down is exercised; 84 (n=1) and 54 (n=2) such all-b_i>0 mismatching instances were found. The empty-index-set case (no row with b_i = 0) is read as the vacuous intersection R^n, the standard reading. Oracle: y in S-polar iff {Ax <= b} union {y^T x > 1} is infeasible, decided exactly and completely by Fourier-Motzkin elimination with strict-inequality tracking over Fraction arithmetic; no floats are used anywhere and no sampling decides anything. The FM core is self-tested on five known feasible/infeasible systems and cross-checked against an independent hand-derived interval oracle on every n=1 instance in the sweep (full agreement); every reported non-membership is additionally backed by an explicit integer witness x in S with y^T x > 1. The one genuine judgement call is that the problem is a pure existence proof ("S polyhedron implies S-polar polyhedron"), which has no algorithmic input/output of its own; the testable object is the solution's own explicit closed-form representation of S-polar, which is what was implemented and refuted.
